figures.shows: Four-stage pipeline: (1) molecular graph embedded as an atom register; (2) quench in the AFM or FM regime (a detuning-versus-Rabi-frequency diagram with an FM star at 2 delta-infinity and an AFM star at delta = 0) and measurement of correlations, diagonal C_ii to node features and C_ij to edge features, with CPU or QPU and the note QPU approximately equal to emulator; (3) hybrid features combining classical RRWP with quantum AFM, FM; (4) training of GNN or transformer backbones (6 backbones plus ESA) on MUTAG (mutagenicity) and ZINC (solubility).
figures.confirmed_by: The complete workflow is presented in Fig. 1.

figures.shows: Four panels of time evolution (x, t from 0 to about 4 microseconds) for one small ZINC-subset molecule. (a) FM diagonal C_ii (y, about 0 to 0.25) and (b) FM off-diagonal C_ij (y, about 0 to 0.1+): traces fluctuate around positive time-average values; (c) AFM diagonal C_ii and (d) AFM off-diagonal C_ij (y, about 0 down to -0.2): AFM off-diagonal values are negative. Dashed lines mark diagonal-ensemble values, squares the finite-time average, triangles the thermal values. The legend names pairs (i,i) = (1,1), (10,10), (0,0), (3,3) and (i,j) = (0,3), (3,8), (0,1), (3,4), (10,11). The molecule graph is drawn in panel (a).

figures.shows: Exploration of the (Omega, delta) parameter space for one molecular graph. Panels (a),(b): off-diagonal correlation weight per node (y) against Omega/J_NN (x, 0 to 1) at delta = 2 delta-infinity (FM, a) and delta = 0 (AFM, b), with curves for the diagonal-ensemble, finite-time average and thermal values and vertical lines at the selected Omega. Panels (c),(d): color maps of the diagonal-ensemble (c) and thermal (d) correlation weight over Omega/J_NN (x, 0 to 1) and delta/delta-infinity (y, -1 to 3), with the line delta = delta-infinity separating the AFM-like and FM-like regimes and a bright band near delta/delta-infinity about 2. Panel (e): absolute effective inverse temperature |beta| J_NN (color scale 0 to about 40), with the two chosen working points marked.
figures.confirmed_by: As predicted by Eq. (23), the line δ = δ∞ separates the AFM-like regime at positive temperature from the FM-like regime at negative temperature.

figures.shows: PCA of quantum features on ZINC-subset in four rows: AFM 1-body, FM 1-body, AFM 2-body, FM 2-body. Left of each row: scree bar chart of variance explained (%) against principal component k (1 to 19) with a cumulative line (0 to 100%). Right: heat map of loadings (timestep 1 to 19 against component 1 to 10). PC1 explains about 80% (1-body) and about 60% (AFM 2-body) to about 77% (FM 2-body); the cumulative line passes 90% within a few components for 1-body and more slowly for 2-body. PC1 loads with one sign across all timesteps while PC2 and PC3 alternate in sign.
figures.confirmed_by: A dominant static component (PC1), capturing the time-averaged correlation strength of each node or edge.

papers.what_it_is: A Pasqal paper (NeurIPS 2026 format) that uses connected occupation correlations from quenched graph-encoded Rydberg Hamiltonians, emulated and run on a neutral-atom QPU for MUTAG, as quantum graph features for GNNs, with an intrinsic probing benchmark, a classical-reconstruction analysis, downstream GNN tests and a synthetic ladder-graph study.

assertions.value: The authors define quantum graph features (QGFs) as the entries of the occupation-based connected correlation matrix: diagonal entries serve as node-level features and off-diagonal entries as pairwise edge-level features.
quotes: The QGFs are defined by the entries of the correlation matrices: diagonal entries provide node-level features, whereas off-diagonal entries provide pairwise edge-level features for the models studied here.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own definition of QGFs in Section 2.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that each graph is encoded into a graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonian, a fixed initial product state evolves under it for a chosen time, and the occupation-based correlation is then measured.
quotes: To obtain QGFs, we encode each graph into a graph-dependent Rydberg Hamiltonian, let a fixed initial product state evolve under this Hamiltonian for a chosen time, after which we measure the desired observable: the occupation-based correlation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own feature-extraction setup in Section 2.

assertions.value: The authors place atoms so that pairs corresponding to graph edges interact strongly, while non-edge pairs are separated far enough that their residual van der Waals interactions are weak.
quotes: The atomic positions are chosen such that pairs of atoms corresponding to graph edges interact strongly, while non-edge pairs are separated far enough that their residual van der Waals interactions are weak.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own embedding setup in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors study molecular graphs from two benchmarks: MUTAG with 188 graphs for binary mutagenicity and ZINCsubset with 12'000 graphs for constrained solubility regression.
quotes: We focus on molecular graphs drawn from two established benchmark datasets: MUTAG (188 graphs, binary mutagenicity) and ZINCsubset(12’000 graphs, constrained solubility regression).
assertions.certainty_reason: Dataset scope stated by the paper in Section 2.2.

assertions.value: The authors report that two-dimensional unit-disk embeddings cover 100% of MUTAG and 95% of ZINCsubset in their datasets.
quotes: In our datasets this covers 100% of MUTAG and 95% of ZINCsubset.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of the datasets that its protocol covers.
assertions.reader_inference: Graphs that need a third dimension are dropped, so ZINC results hold for the embeddable 95% only.

quotes: The current limitations are clear. The encoding

assertions.value: The authors state that the choice of the FM detuning at twice the infinite-temperature detuning cancels the spatially averaged longitudinal field, and that the AFM detuning of zero lies below the infinite-temperature detuning, in the positive-temperature regime.
quotes: The choice δ = 0 places the AFM setting below δ∞ and hence in the positive-temperature regime of Eq. (23).
The choice δ = 2δ∞ places the FM setting in the negative-temperature regime and it has an additional useful interpretation: it cancels the spatially averaged longitudinal field.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own quench-parameter setup and its rationale in Appendix C.

assertions.value: The authors state that increasing the detuning moves the thermal interpretation from an AFM-like positive-temperature regime through infinite temperature into an FM-like negative-temperature regime, and that this classification does not imply thermalization for all values of the pulse parameters.
quotes: Thus, increasing the detuning moves the thermal interpretation from an AFM-like positive-temperature regime through infinite temperature into an FM-like negative-temperature regime.
This classification does not imply that the system thermalizes for all values of (Ω, δ);
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of their thermal argument.
assertions.reader_inference: The criterion follows from the monotonicity of thermal energy shown in Appendix B (Eqs. 20 and 21), which the paper derives without naming a theorem.

assertions.value: The authors state that the canonical thermal approximation is used as a diagnostic tool for selecting quench parameters and is not assumed to hold throughout the full parameter space.
quotes: This approximation is used in Sec. 2.3 and App. C as a diagnostic tool for selecting quench parameters (Ω, δ). It is not assumed to hold throughout the full parameter space.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the limit of their thermalization argument.

assertions.value: The authors state that the AFM setting is chosen more empirically, with detuning zero, and that the Rabi frequency 0.3 J_NN/hbar yields a similar effective temperature scale and lies in a region with pronounced negative off-diagonal correlations.
quotes: The AFM setting is chosen more empirically.
We then choose Ω = 0.3 JNN/ℏ, which yields a similar effective temperature scale and lies in a region with pronounced negative off-diagonal correlations, as shown in Fig. 4(c).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own AFM working point was chosen.

assertions.value: The authors state that they select the Rabi frequency 0.5 J_NN/hbar for the FM setting, slightly above the thermal-maximum value, because it remains in a regime of enhanced correlations while producing more robust dynamical relaxation.
quotes: We therefore select the slightly larger value Ω = 0.5 JNN/ℏ [cf. Eq. (4) or (24)], which remains in a regime of enhanced correlations while producing more robust dynamical relaxation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states how its own FM working point was chosen.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the molecular graph of Figure 4 the thermal correlation maximum appears near a Rabi frequency of about 0.23 J_NN/hbar and a detuning of about 2.1 times the infinite-temperature detuning, which they interpret as a finite-size thermal crossover.
quotes: For the graph considered in Fig. 4, the thermal correlation maximum appears near Ω/(JNN/ℏ) ≈ 0.23 and δ/δ∞ ≈ 2.1, which we interpret as a finite-size thermal crossover.
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-graph numerical scan whose interpretation is the authors' own.
